cpl129_wright_1995.title: Donald Wright, “Discourse, Power and Tradition: Approach and Method in Recent English-Canadian Intellectual History,” Acadiensis 24, no. 2 (Spring 1995): 122–34.
cpl129_wright_1995.citation: Donald Wright, “Discourse, Power and Tradition: Approach and Method in Recent English-Canadian Intellectual History,” Acadiensis 24, no. 2 (Spring 1995): 122–34.

verification.note: Review essay on six other books (Valverde, Anderson, Vipond, Ferguson, Christian, Horton); The Quest of the Folk is not among them. Page 122 (opening, three approaches: discourse analysis, history of political thought, biography) and p. 132 read. Note 29 (p. 132): 'For a very skilled handling of Antonio Gramsci's theory of cultural hegemony by an historian see Ian McKay, The Quest of the Folk ... (Montreal and Kingston, 1994).' This is a footnote recommendation, not a review of the book. Checked against: UNB Libraries Acadiensis article page and PDF (article/view/12013; PDF 12013/12857). Addendum 2026-10-14: Valverde section re-read for the 1.135 person entry, pp. 122–126 (UNB PDF 12013/12857). Wright reviews The Age of Light, Soap, and Water as one of six books. Passages used: 'In her much talked about treatise'; the six authors include 'one a sociologist (Mariana Valverde)'; 'Following Foucault' (p. 122); 'Valverde is quick to avoid a "descent into discourse"'; she 'modifies Foucault's archaeology' and 'maintains an important commitment to social agency'; quotes the book's p. 43 on 'the decentring of the subject' (p. 123); quotes p. 166, '[m]oral regulation is an important aspect of ruling, helping to constitute class, gender, sexual, and race relations'; 'the concept of slippages', 'her most exciting, most original, contribution' (p. 124); her conclusion that audiences 'knew precisely what was meant' is 'untenable'; 'the impoverished immigrant and the "fallen woman" remain conspicuously silent' (p. 125); 'the silence of the consumer amidst the din of the producer gives the impression of top-down social control, precisely what Valverde sought to avoid' (p. 126). Addendum 2026-10-26: Fresh 2026-10-26 UNB PDF 122–129 and 132/n29 selected passages rechecked. Wright’s actual Lears uses at 124/n7, 127/n16 and 129/n21 are separate from his McKay footnote recommendation 132/n29. Wright lacks endpoint; substantive Lears resource explicitly held. No inference he reviewed Quest.

pe135_valverde_deconstructive_1995.citation: Mariana Valverde, “Deconstructive Marxism,” review essay on Jacques Derrida, Specters of Marx (1994), Labour/Le Travail 36 (Fall 1995): 329–340.

verification.note: Journal PDF (lltjournal.ca article 5013, galley 5882; citation line on p. 329: Labour/Le Travail, 36 (Fall 1995), 329-40). Pages 329–332 read; the rest searched by keyword only. Passages used: 'Joan Scott made an influential attempt to extend the reach of deconstruction within historical writing to the certainties of class. Her argument was limited in many ways' (pp. 331–332); 'Scott probably used her new-found theories to justify a break with Marxism that she, like so many other former leftists on both sides of the Atlantic, wanted to make anyway'; 'Scott's rather exaggerated claims about what great male French theorists can do for feminism'; the book's contribution made 'at the expense of working-class history'; 'for many labour historians, any hint of theoretical sophistication became prima faciae evidence of political backsliding'; n. 5 names Palmer's Descent into Discourse as 'the by now standard Marxist critique of Scott' (all p. 332).

pe135_valverde_deconstructive_1995.scope_note: In-period: her later judgment of Scott and of the discourse debate in Canadian labour history.
